items.abstract: <jats:p>The paper deals with the problem of learning tasks, where the robot is in permanent contact with the environment. We propose a new strategy based on a hierarchical learning scheme and representation of the task as a directed graph. The graph is built of nodes and branches, which correspond to the states and actions, respectively.The upper hierarchical level is essentially a decision-making algorithm. Optimal decision-making is supported using reinforcement learning (RL) techniques. The actions are generated by a constraint-space following (CSF) controller, which autonomously looks for directions where motion is possible. The controller generates robot motion by adjusting its stiffness in the direction defined by the Frenet-Serret frame attached to the robot path.The proposed framework was experimentally verified on challenging robot tasks such as maze learning, door opening, learning to shift the manual car gear, and learning car licence  plate light assembly by disassembly.</jats:p>
title: Hierarchical Learning of Robotic Contact Policies

items.abstract: This chapter discusses the Autumn 1921 issue of the Little Review, which announced a new direction for the journal. The issue was described as a “protest” by international writers and artists against the magazine's prosecution in the Ulysses case. The chapter explains that the Autumn 1921 issue was called the “Brâncuşi number” because it contained twenty reproductions of the Romanian sculptor's abstract work and was accompanied by an appreciative essay by Ezra Pound. The chapter also details how Margaret Anderson felt some of the pressures on her lift after she and Jane Heap compromised by issuing the Little Review as a quarterly. Despite the Little Review's setbacks, the Autumn 1921 issue demonstrated that the magazine was not running on its final fumes and it foreshadowed a torrent of the most genuinely avantgarde work done on the international stage.
